name: Dimensional Formula
description: Writing the units of a quantity in terms of base units (using M, L, T, etc.)

content.overview: Saying 'kilograms times meters squared divided by seconds squared' out loud is a mouthful. Physicists got tired of it too, so they came up with a shorthand code: **[M L² T⁻²]**. That's a dimensional formula — think of it as a unit's ID tag. {{viz:diagram-01}}
content.explanation:
Let's crack the code. {{viz:diagram-02}}

**The symbols everyone agrees on:**
- M = Mass (kilogram)
- L = Length (meter)
- T = Time (second)
- I = Electric current (ampere)
- θ = Temperature (kelvin)
- n = Amount (mole)
- J = Luminous intensity (candela)

**Writing one yourself is easier than it looks:**

Just take the unit and swap in the symbols, keeping track of the powers.

**Speed:** m/s = L/T = **[L T⁻¹]**

**Force:** kg·m/s² = M·L·T⁻² = **[M L T⁻²]**

**Energy:** kg·m²/s² = M·L²·T⁻² = **[M L² T⁻²]**

**Acceleration:** m/s² = L/T² = **[L T⁻²]** {{viz:chart-01}}

**Why bother with this code at all?** {{viz:anim-01}}

1. **It's way shorter** — [M L² T⁻²] beats spelling out the whole phrase every time
2. **It's a quick X-ray** — instantly see which base units built a derived unit
3. **It powers dimensional analysis** — makes checking equations painless
4. **It's universal** — no translating needed, every physicist on Earth reads the same symbols

**The quick rule:** write the base-unit symbol, then its power. No power written means power 1. Division just flips the sign to negative.
keyPoints: A dimensional formula is a symbol-based shorthand for a unit
M stands for mass, L for length, T for time
It's always written in brackets, like [M L² T⁻²]
It shows exactly which base units built up a quantity
Division shows up as a negative power (T⁻² means divided by T²)
It's a shorthand every physicist worldwide understands the same way
content.whyItMatters: Once you can read dimensional formulas, you can eyeball any quantity and instantly know what it's made of — and use that to sanity-check whether an equation actually makes sense. It's notation you'll run into constantly.
